definition: A text-only way to control a computer by typing commands. Attackers like it because it can be scripted and leaves little on screen.
The channel an attacker uses to send orders to a compromised machine and get results back. Defenders look for it by spotting odd network traffic.
Hopping from one compromised machine to others on the same network. It is how a small foothold grows into a big breach.
What an account is allowed to do on a system. Attackers want more of it, such as administrator or root.
A secret that proves who you are, such as a password, key or token. Stolen credentials let attackers log in like a normal user.
The part of an attack that does the harmful work once it is running. It might steal files, encrypt data or open a backdoor.
Techniques that keep an attacker's access alive after a reboot or password change. Examples are scheduled tasks and startup entries.
Secretly copying data out of a victim's network to the attacker. It is often disguised as normal traffic.
A Windows process that holds logon secrets in memory. Attackers dump its memory to steal passwords and hashes.
Windows' central database of settings. Attackers edit it to run programs at startup or change security settings.
A job the system runs automatically at set times. Attackers use them to run their code again and again.
Tricking someone with a fake message into clicking a link, opening a file or giving up a password. Spearphishing targets one person or group.
Software written to cause harm, such as stealing data or taking control. Viruses, trojans and ransomware are all malware.
A hidden way back into a system that skips the normal login. Attackers plant one so they can return later.
Making code or data hard to read so tools and analysts can't easily understand it. It is used to dodge detection.
A powerful Windows command-line shell and scripting language. Attackers favour it because it is built in and can do almost anything.
A built-in Windows feature for managing and querying computers, locally or remotely. Attackers use it to run commands on other machines.
A set of rules that lets one program ask another to do something. Attackers call APIs to do things like inject code or read files.
Running malicious code inside another program's memory. It hides the attacker behind a trusted process name.
A fixed-length fingerprint made from data by a one-way function. Passwords are stored as hashes, and file hashes identify known malware.
A running instance of a program. Security tools watch processes to spot suspicious behaviour.
A Windows file of code that programs load and share. Attackers trick programs into loading a malicious one.
A small piece of machine code that an attacker injects and runs, often to get a shell. It is usually the first stage of an attack.
Going from a low-powered account to a more powerful one. It often uses a software bug or a misconfiguration.
Logging in with a stolen password hash instead of the password itself. It works because some systems accept the hash as proof.
Guessing many passwords until one works. Spraying tries a few common passwords across many accounts to avoid lockouts.
Software that secretly records what a person types. It is used to capture passwords and messages.
Malware that locks or encrypts files and demands payment to restore them. Some also threaten to leak stolen data.
Malware that gives an attacker remote control of a machine. It can watch the screen, run commands and move files.
A small program whose only job is to install other malware. It keeps the first stage small and easy to hide.
Code that loads and starts the main malware, often decrypting it first. It is a common way to slip past scanners.
A regular check-in from malware to its C2 server, like a heartbeat. Steady timing is a clue defenders look for.
Wrapping one kind of traffic inside another to sneak past firewalls. DNS and HTTPS tunnels are common.
A middleman server that passes traffic along. Attackers use proxies to hide where their traffic really comes from.
Using tools already on the victim's system instead of bringing new malware. It blends in with normal admin work.
Microsoft's directory service that manages users, computers and permissions in a company. Controlling it often means controlling the whole network.
A ticket-based login system used in Windows domains. Attackers steal or forge tickets to impersonate users.
An older Windows login method based on password hashes. It is weak and often abused for relaying and pass-the-hash.
A digital pass that says who you are and what you can do. Stealing one lets an attacker act as you without a password.
Logging in with more than a password, such as a phone code. It makes stolen passwords far less useful.
A locked-down space for running code safely. Some malware checks for one and stays quiet if it finds it.
Software that looks for and blocks malware. EDR also records endpoint activity so defenders can investigate.
A record of events on a system. Attackers sometimes delete logs to cover their tracks.
A flaw in software that can be abused. An exploit is the code that takes advantage of it.
A flaw the vendor doesn't know about yet, so no fix exists. Attackers prize them for that reason.
Attacking a trusted supplier so the harm reaches its customers. A poisoned software update is a classic case.
The server that checks logins in a Windows domain. Taking it over gives an attacker the keys to the network.
The internet's phone book that turns names into addresses. Attackers abuse it to find targets and hide traffic.
Scrambling data so only someone with the key can read it. Attackers use it to hide traffic or hold files to ransom.
A script planted on a web server that lets an attacker run commands through a web page. It gives them a quiet way back in.
A small program embedded in an Office document. Malicious ones run when the victim enables them.
A more specific version of a technique in ATT&CK. For example PowerShell is a sub-technique of Command and Scripting Interpreter.
